tier_reason: Only vendor numbers exist, read from WebSearch snippets of the Cheerp 2.6rc1 release post (Emscripten's public benchmark suite: Box2D, Bullet, zlib, LZMA vs Emscripten 2.0.9 on SpiderMonkey and V8, one MacBook Pro, mean of 3 runs); flags and CPU model are not stated and the post could not be opened, so first-party snippet-only evidence stays C. Neither the cheerp-compiler nor the cheerp-meta README carries a benchmark (cheerp-meta only says 'best performing ... compiler available on the market', no numbers).

corrections.workload: Vendor release-post comparison on Emscripten's own benchmark suite (Box2D, Bullet, zlib, LZMA) compiled with Cheerp 2.6rc1 and Emscripten 2.0.9, run on SpiderMonkey and V8, one MacBook Pro (Linux x86_64, TurboBoost disabled), averaged over three runs (snippet only; the post could not be opened)
corrections.hardware: MacBook Pro, Linux x86_64, TurboBoost disabled (CPU model not stated; snippet only)
corrections.is_fork_of: llvm/llvm-project (downstream fork of LLVM/Clang carrying the full LLVM history; not marked as a GitHub fork)
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: leaningtech.com, new.leaningtech.com and labs.leaningtech.com did not resolve from this environment, so the speed claim comes from WebSearch snippets of vendor posts. The 5% figure is from the Cheerp 2.6rc1 post (December 2020 era, against Emscripten 2.0.9) and the same snippets give output about 3% smaller; the later Cheerp 3.0 post (March 2023, when Cheerp was relicensed from GPLv2/commercial to Apache-2.0 with LLVM exception) claims about 7% smaller output and execution speed comparable to Emscripten, i.e. parity, not a win. The only independent comparisons found (Palant 2016; i-programmer, Cheerp 1.x) are asm.js-era and had Emscripten ahead or equal. No benchmark in the cheerp-compiler or cheerp-meta READMEs; compiler flags and CPU model never stated. Treat as weak: smaller output, about equal speed.

notes: Record is accurate; claim is marginal (5% faster in a 2020 vendor post, parity in the 2023 vendor post) and snippet-only. The vendor post URL set as benchmark_url came from WebSearch results and could not be opened (DNS failure for new.leaningtech.com); license Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception confirmed from LICENSE.TXT and the cheerp-meta README, last commit 2026-10-09 and 363 stars confirmed. Shortcomings: vendor-only, snippet-only, near-parity, stale baseline version, no flags or CPU model.

tier_reason: A first-party benchmark repo exists (moonbit-community/benchmark-202404: bench_iter/bench.mjs and bench_json5/bench.mjs with tinybench, precompiled MoonBit JS committed) and states Node v22.0.0 and an Apple M2 Max, with build command 'moon build --target js' in package.json; the MoonBit compiler version is not stated, so it falls just short of A and stays C (first-party). The record's own fib/compile-time numbers are snippet-only relays of vendor posts and were replaced.

corrections.baseline: Plain JavaScript in Node v22.0.0 (V8): an idiomatic Array flatMap/filter/map/reduce chain and the same chain on JS Iterator Helpers, plus the json5 npm library's parse; vendor snippets also compare wasm output against Rust and Go compiled to WebAssembly
corrections.workload: MoonBit JS-backend output vs plain JS in Node v22.0.0 (tinybench, warmup then run): bench_iter runs a flat_map/filter/map/map/filter/fold pipeline over a JSON class/member dataset; bench_json5 parses data/data.json5 with MoonBit core's json5 package (compiled to JS) versus json5.parse from npm. Precompiled MoonBit JS is committed in the repo (April 2024).
corrections.claimed_speedup: benchmark-202404 README (Node v22.0.0, MBP 2023 Apple M2 Max): iter 2,953,032 ops/s MoonBit vs 383,701 Plain JS (7.7x, derived from page data), 117,733 JS Iterator Helpers (25.1x, derived from page data; the source of the vendor's 'up to 25x faster than native JS' headline) and 155,935 Kotlin/JS; json5 22,908 ops/s MoonbitJson5.parse vs 2,887 json5.parse (7.9x, derived from page data). Snippet only, not checked: fib(46) run ten million times as wasm, MoonBit 177.9 ms vs Rust 160.8 ms vs Go 6357.8 ms (slower than Rust); 626 packages compiled in 1.06 s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: moon build --target js (release output under target/js/release, per bench_iter/package.json and bench_json5/package.json); MoonBit compiler version not stated; JS baselines run as-is on Node v22.0.0
corrections.caveats: Benchmark is first-party (moonbit-community, April 2024, MoonBit pre-1.0) and runs MoonBit's JS backend, not its wasm backend. The iter baseline is an eager Array chain that allocates an intermediate array per stage while MoonBit's Iter is a fused push-style pipeline; no hand-written JS loop baseline is included, so the 7.7x/25x figures measure iteration strategy more than language. The json5 row compares two different parser implementations (MoonBit's port returns MoonBit JsonValue with a persistent map, json5 builds JS objects), and the harness discards the return value without checking that parse returned Ok; a zenn.dev reviewer (snippet only) attributes the json5 gain to char-code handling that hand-written JS could copy. MoonBit compiler version not stated. The fib(46) and compile-time numbers are snippet-only relays of vendor posts (moonbitlang.com and thenewstack.io unreachable) and show MoonBit slower than Rust. Licensing: moonbitlang/core is Apache-2.0, but the compiler (moonbitlang/moonbit-compiler) is under the MoonBit Public License, a non-OSI 'relaxed SSPL' that allows modification only for non-commercial use, and its wasm backend is not open-sourced; compiled artifacts may be licensed freely.

notes: Upgraded evidence within tier C: found the vendor's public benchmark repo moonbit-community/benchmark-202404 comparing MoonBit's JS backend against plain JS in V8 (in-list baseline), 7.7x-25x on an iterator pipeline and 7.9x on JSON5 parsing; near-A except for the missing MoonBit compiler version. Shortcomings for the record: eager-array JS baseline vs fused iterators, different json5 parser implementations with unchecked results, JS backend rather than wasm, first-party, numbers from April 2024; compiler licence is non-OSI so usability set to mixed. Stars 1.2k, Apache-2.0 and last commit 2026-10-11 confirmed for moonbitlang/core.

tier_reason: The repo's benchmark runner (demo/benchmark/index.js, benchmarkRunner.js) times the same core as AssemblyScript Wasm vs TypeScript-compiled JS vs TS+Closure JS, but no numbers are committed and the first-party Medium article is unreachable. Search snippets of a peer-reviewed study (De Macedo, Abreu, Pereira, Saraiva, 'WebAssembly versus JavaScript: Energy and Runtime Performance', 2022, IEEE) report WasmBoy as its real-world benchmark with Wasm faster than JS; snippet-only numbers cap it at C (upgraded from D), a candidate for B once the paper or thesis PDF is readable.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No numbers in the repo; the first-party Medium article ('WebAssembly is fast: a real-world benchmark of WebAssembly vs ES6', 2019) could not be fetched. Snippet only: De Macedo et al. 2022 ran six Game Boy games on WasmBoy in Chrome, Edge and Firefox (36 samples, Wasm core vs TypeScript-compiled JS core) and report Wasm faster in their regression model, with a language factor of 0.84 for Wasm vs 1 for JavaScript; the same study reports Firefox often favouring JavaScript (stated for its micro-benchmarks).
corrections.workload: Game Boy / Game Boy Color emulator core frame throughput: the same AssemblyScript source built as Wasm (AssemblyScript compiler), as JS through the TypeScript compiler (memory interface mocked) and as TS plus Closure Compiler, timed per frame in the browser by demo/benchmark (optional extra cores: binjgb C compiled with Emscripten, GameBoy Online in JS)
corrections.caveats: No figures in the README; benchmark_url is the README section, which links the benchmark app (wasmboy.app, unreachable) and a 2019 Medium article (unreachable). The only numbers seen are WebSearch snippets of the De Macedo et al. 2022 study (master's thesis at repositorium.sdum.uminho.pt, paper behind IEEE paywall), which used WasmBoy as its real-world benchmark; snippets do not state CPU model or versions and one summary was unsure whether the study used WasmBoy itself or only its harness design. Toolchain is old (assemblyscript ^0.15.1, typescript ^3.1.3); last real development before the October 2022 dependency bumps. GPL-3.0-or-later (copyleft).

notes: Confirmed and upgraded D to C on snippet-only peer-reviewed evidence; record as a paper-access retier candidate to B (De Macedo et al. 2022, thesis PDF https://repositorium.sdum.uminho.pt/bitstream/1822/86805/1/Joao%20Goncalves%20De%20Macedo.pdf, DNS-blocked here).
